title: "At Home in Space" opens, caps Air and Space Museum renovation
gist: The Smithsonian finished a seven-year, nearly $1 billion renovation of the National Air and Space Museum's flagship building with the October 30 opening of 'At Home in Space', a gallery on long-duration spaceflight. It includes the only fully flown EMU spacesuit on public display and a space reserved for the Artemis I capsule.

insights.claim: After seven years and nearly $1 billion, the Smithsonian has completed the renovation of the National Air and Space Museum's flagship building in Washington, DC.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: This is a large public investment in aerospace heritage and outreach.

insights.claim: Curator Jennifer Levasseur says the gallery covers preparation, the space shuttle, 25-plus years of long-duration ISS experience, and next steps toward bases on the Moon and Mars.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: It reflects how institutions frame the shift from visiting space to living there.

insights.claim: The gallery shows what Levasseur believes is the first and possibly only public display of a fully flown EMU spacesuit set, missing only a functioning PLSS backpack because all the backpacks are still needed.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: Decades-old EMU hardware is still in active use, which shows how slowly spacesuits get replaced.

insights.claim: The EMU suits introduced early in the space shuttle program are still used for US spacewalks on the ISS.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: Legacy suit dependence points to the need for next-generation suit development.

insights.claim: The exhibit includes the first 3D printer used in space, flown in 2014 by Made In Space, now part of Redwire, and NASA, which produced hundreds of objects including tools and repair parts.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: It is historical validation of in-space manufacturing, a capability Redwire now owns.

insights.claim: The gallery ends with a space reserved for the Artemis I capsule, held for now by a Lockheed Martin scale model of Orion until NASA delivers the real spacecraft, which is expected later this year.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: Artemis hardware is moving into heritage displays, which reinforces public visibility of the program.

insights.claim: Recovered Challenger and Columbia components on display make this only the second public exhibit of fallen orbiter debris, after a 2015 Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex exhibit.
insights.speaker: Robert Pearlman
insights.so_what: It is a reminder of the safety record that shapes risk tolerance in human spaceflight.
